issues.legal_issue: A bail order may be cancelled on appeal where the seriousness of the allegations, the prima facie case, the accused persons’ position and the risks to witnesses justify cancellation, even without proof that bail was misused.
material_facts: The appellants were police personnel charged in connection with an alleged conspiracy to abduct and kill a person and present the death as a police encounter.
A magistrate’s inquiry and the investigation produced material indicating that the deceased had been abducted while in police custody, killed, and that a false encounter account had been recorded.

Station diary entries, the accused persons’ recorded accounts of being part of the encounter team, and other investigation material provided a prima facie basis for the alleged involvement of several appellants.
A witness was allegedly detained by police, and the accused persons’ position and alleged conduct gave rise to a risk that witnesses or their relatives could be threatened or harmed.
The Sessions Court granted bail, and the High Court cancelled it; the appellants challenged that cancellation on the ground that bail could be cancelled only for misuse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in cancelling bail, and the appeals were dismissed. The Court’s assessment was for the bail question only and did not determine the criminal case, which the trial court was to decide independently.
issues.legal_principle: There is no absolute rule that bail may be cancelled only upon proof of misuse. The court considering cancellation must assess the circumstances, including the gravity and nature of the offence, the prima facie case, the accused persons’ position and standing, and other relevant risks. The distinction between granting bail and cancelling it, discussed in Bhagirathsinh s/o Mahipat Singh Judeja v. State of Gujarat (1984) 1 SCC 284, Dolat Ram v. State of Haryana (1995) 1 SCC 349, and Ramcharan v. State of M.P. (2004) 13 SCC 617, is not an absolute rule; the principle concerning an application to the same court does not govern an appeal against the order granting bail.

rule.if: bail_grant_appealed and serious_offence_allegations and prima_facie_involvement and (official_role_abused or witness_safety_risk)

predicates.bail_grant_appealed: A criminal appeal challenges an order granting bail.
predicates.serious_offence_allegations: The accused are alleged to have participated in a grave offence.
predicates.prima_facie_involvement: The available material provides a prima facie basis for the accused persons’ involvement.
predicates.official_role_abused: The accused are alleged to have used positions of public authority to participate in criminal conduct.
predicates.witness_safety_risk: The accused persons’ conduct or position gives rise to a risk that witnesses or their relatives may be threatened or harmed.

issues.definition: When an appealed bail grant concerns serious allegations supported by a prima facie case, and the accused allegedly abused public authority or pose a risk to witness safety, cancellation of the grant is justified.
